aboutH2: Alberta Adolescent Recovery Centre: Long-Term Youth Addiction Treatment in Calgary
intro: The Alberta Adolescent Recovery Centre (AARC) is a long-term treatment program for adolescents suffering from substance dependency. The AARC program is often the last resort for addicted youth (ages 12-21) and their families who have exhausted numerous social agencies and treatment programs, with little to no success. The AARC program is divided into structured stages of treatment that are designed to help clients attain specific milestones in their recovery. As the client progresses through the stages, they are given more responsibilities and are gradually reintegrated back into society. The stages have corresponding AA/NA steps that our clients learn in order to gain daily living coping skills that replace dependence on drugs and/or alcohol. Each client completes the AARC program at their own pace but on average, clients finish the program in 8 to 10 months.

pillars.title: A Day Centre in Southeast Calgary, With Nights in Family Homes
pillars.body: AARC runs from 303 Forge Road SE, in the Fairview industrial area of southeast Calgary just south of Glenmore Trail. Youth spend their days here. The building has a full kitchen where chefs cook meals through the day, a fitness centre where clients train with a personal trainer three times a week, an activity room, an outdoor hockey rink and basketball courts. At night nobody sleeps at the centre. Youth stay in recovery homes, which are the private homes of families further along in the program. AARC trains the host families, checks each home, has the homes accredited by the Canadian Accreditation Council and keeps someone on call around the clock.

pillars.title: Back to School or Work, Then a Community That Stays
pillars.body: The last of AARC's four levels moves youth back into school or work while the family keeps getting support. Graduation is not a hard stop. Youth and parents can keep using AARC's services afterwards, and the centre encourages them to stay involved by helping families who are just starting. Some graduate families go on to open their own homes as recovery homes, and many of the peer counsellors on staff finished the program themselves.

pillars.title: Peer Counsellors Working With a Clinical Team
pillars.body: Executive Director Donny Serink, a registered social worker with a master's in social work, took over in October 2025 after ten years in clinical and leadership roles at AARC. Dr. Dean Vause, whose PhD research shaped the treatment model, is now Senior Advisor. The centre says most of its staff are graduates of the program. Every client gets a peer mentor in recovery, and the team also includes clinical and family counsellors, a registered nurse and a licensed practical nurse. Two consulting psychiatrists, Dr. Lori Hogg and Dr. Elizabeth Wallace, and psychologist Joel Mader work with the team, and Dr. Hogg can prescribe when a youth needs medication.

overviewH2: Alberta Adolescent Recovery Centre: Centre Overview
overview: AARC is a non-profit program for 12 to 21 year olds with serious alcohol or drug problems, and it treats the whole family alongside the young person. Treatment follows the 12 steps of Alcoholics Anonymous in four levels and aims at full abstinence. Youth have individual and group counselling several times a day with social workers, certified addiction counsellors, clinical counsellors and peer staff. The centre also supports concurrent mental health problems, with nursing care and consulting psychiatrists and psychologists. Most families stay 8 to 10 months, though nobody is pushed out on a fixed date.

afterOverview: AARC was set up in Calgary in 1990 and took its first youth in 1992, with funding from the Government of Alberta and a donation from the Rotary Club of Calgary. Today it is partly funded by the province's Ministry of Mental Health and Addiction, with the rest coming from donors and fundraising events. In 2015 a $300,000 grant paid for an independent evaluation led by Dr. Amelia Arria of the University of Maryland. The centre reports that 80.5% of clients who entered treatment completed it, and that 73% of graduates said they were still abstinent 12 months after graduating, falling to 59% at 24 months. These figures came from retrospective interviews with a sample of past clients.

location.heading: Alberta Adolescent Recovery Centre in Calgary, Alberta
location.intro: AARC is at 303 Forge Road SE in the Fairview industrial area of southeast Calgary, close to Glenmore Trail and Macleod Trail and about 15 minutes by car from downtown and the Beltline. Families come from across Southern Alberta: Chestermere is about 25 minutes away, Okotoks about 30, Airdrie and Cochrane around 35 to 40, Red Deer about an hour and 45 minutes and Edmonton roughly three hours up Highway 2.

faqIntro: Answers come from the centre's listing and its own website. Still unsure? Call, it's free and confidential.

faqs.q: How much does the Alberta Adolescent Recovery Centre cost?
faqs.a: AARC does not publish a set price. Fees are worked out for each family based on what it can afford, because the program is partly funded by the Government of Alberta's Ministry of Mental Health and Addiction and by donors. The centre says no one who needs the program is turned away because they cannot cover the cost.

AARC treats youth and young adults aged 12 to 21 who meet the criteria for a substance use disorder. Many also have mental health or behavioural problems, which the program is set up to support. The young person has to be between 12 and 21 when they enter treatment.

faqs.q: Do parents have to take part?
faqs.a: Yes. A parent, guardian or loved one must support the young person and take part for the whole program, and AARC says this is mandatory. Family members get their own counselling as the youth moves through the four levels, and siblings are included too.

faqs.q: How long is the AARC program?
faqs.a: Most families spend 8 to 10 months in treatment. The program is not time limited, so a youth moves through the four levels at their own pace and graduates when they are ready.

AARC is semi-residential. Youth spend their days at the centre in southeast Calgary, then spend nights in recovery homes, which are the private homes of families further along in the program. AARC trains the host families and provides 24/7 on-call support, and the homes are accredited by the Canadian Accreditation Council.

faqs.q: How do we get started, and do we need a referral?
faqs.a: You do not need a referral. Admission starts with a phone call to (403) 253-5250, where the intake team gathers information about your family. If you want to go ahead, the clinical team takes you through AARC's youth-focused assessment. The centre's website also has a free online questionnaire about early signs of addiction.

faqs.q: Who works with the young people at AARC?
faqs.a: AARC says the majority of its staff are graduates of the program, and every client is paired with a peer mentor who is in recovery. The clinical side includes social workers, clinical and family counsellors, certified addiction counsellors, a registered nurse and a licensed practical nurse. Consulting psychiatrists Dr. Lori Hogg and Dr. Elizabeth Wallace and psychologist Joel Mader also work with the team.

faqs.q: Does AARC help with mental health problems as well as addiction?
faqs.a: Yes. AARC says its model supports concurrent mental health disorders, with care from its nursing team and consulting psychiatry and psychology professionals. Its consulting child and adolescent psychiatrist sees clients and families and can prescribe medication when needed.

No, AARC does not list detox or medical withdrawal management among its services, and its recovery.com profile marks detox as not offered. If your child needs to withdraw safely first, ask the intake team how to arrange that before treatment starts.

faqs.q: Where is AARC and how do we get there?
faqs.a: AARC is at 303 Forge Road SE, Calgary, in the Fairview industrial area south of Glenmore Trail. It is about 15 minutes by car from downtown Calgary, around 30 minutes from Okotoks and 35 to 40 minutes from Airdrie or Cochrane. The office is open Monday to Friday, 8am to 5pm.

After graduation, youth and their families can keep using AARC's services and stay part of its community. Many go on to mentor new families, and some open their homes as recovery homes for youth starting the program. The goal set during treatment is a return to school or work with sobriety that lasts.

Yes. AARC is licensed as a Residential Addiction Treatment Service Provider under Alberta's Mental Health Services Protection Act, as its website states. It is also accredited by the Canadian Accreditation Council of Human Services for its recovery homes, day treatment, community services and governance, valid until February 2027.
